title: Fit a curve, check it, standardise a reading, count the yes results

items.prompt: A renal clinic records serum creatinine for its outpatients and adopts a normal model with mean 96 micromol/L and standard deviation 14 micromol/L. Give the upper boundary of the band that lies two standard deviations above the mean, in micromol/L.

answer.reasoning: Two standard deviations above the mean is 96 + 2 × 14 = 96 + 28 = 124 micromol/L. The corresponding lower boundary is 96 − 28 = 68, and the empirical rule places 95.45 per cent of the modelled values between them.
commonErrors: Answering 110, which adds one standard deviation instead of two.
Answering 138, which adds three standard deviations because the 99.7 per cent figure was recalled instead of the 95 per cent one.

items.prompt: Under a normal model for fasting glucose with mean 142 mg/dL and standard deviation 18 mg/dL, what is the probability that a randomly chosen person's fasting glucose is exactly 142 mg/dL?

options.text: Zero, because a single value spans no width and encloses no area under the curve.
It is the highest probability of any value, because 142 is where the curve peaks.
About 0.68, because 142 is the mean and the empirical rule assigns 68 per cent there.
About 1 in 60, because the cohort has 60 people and one of them could be at the mean.

answer.reasoning: For a continuous distribution, probability is area under the curve between two values. A single point has no width, so it encloses no area and its probability is zero. The curve's height at 142 is a probability density, which is at its maximum there, and a density is not a probability. The 68 per cent figure applies to the whole band from 124 to 160, not to the centre point. The 1 in 60 answer confuses a question about the model with a question about the sample in hand.
acceptableResponses: 0, because probability is area and a point has no width.
commonErrors: Reading the peak height of the curve as the probability of the mean.
Attaching the 68 per cent band figure to the single value at its centre.

items.prompt: In the study cohort fasting glucose has mean 142 mg/dL and standard deviation 18 mg/dL. Give the z-score of a reading of 169 mg/dL, to two decimal places.

answer.reasoning: Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation: (169 − 142) ÷ 18 = 27 ÷ 18 = 1.50. The reading sits one and a half standard deviations above the centre of this cohort. The answer carries no units, because the mg/dL in the numerator and the denominator cancel.
commonErrors: Answering 27, which is the raw distance from the mean rather than the distance in standard deviations.
Answering 9.39 by dividing the reading by the standard deviation without subtracting the mean first.

items.prompt: A colleague writes in a report: "Patient K's fasting glucose has a z-score of +1.4, so about 92 per cent of comparable patients have a lower reading." Two separate things are missing before that percentage claim can be assessed. Name both, and say why each one matters.

answer.correct: The reference distribution the score was computed against, and the check that the reference distribution is the right shape before the score is turned into a probability.
answer.summary: The reference group is unnamed, and the shape needed to convert distance into a percentile has not been established.
answer.reasoning: A z-score is a distance from the centre of a particular distribution, so the same reading standardises differently against a cohort of people with diagnosed type 2 diabetes, centred near 142 mg/dL, and against a general screening population centred nearer 104 mg/dL. Without the reference group named, +1.4 cannot be converted back into a glucose value or compared with anyone else's score. Separately, the stated 92 per cent is a percentile conversion read from a normal curve. If the reference distribution is right-skewed, as fasting plasma glucose is in a general population, the distance survives and the asserted percentage does not. A strong answer also notes that neither problem is fixed by more decimal places.
acceptableResponses: The reference distribution is not stated, and its shape has not been checked, so the distance cannot be interpreted or converted into a probability.
Which population the mean and standard deviation came from, and whether that population's distribution is actually normal.
commonErrors: Naming only the missing reference group and treating the conversion from z to a percentage as automatic.
Answering that the units are missing, when a z-score correctly has none.
Treating +1.4 as a percentile on its own, when a z-score reports distance and a percentile additionally requires a distributional shape.

items.prompt: A hospital biochemistry service fits a normal model to 500 serum triglyceride results, obtaining a mean of 1.5 mmol/L and a standard deviation of 0.9 mmol/L. It then counts how many results fall in each region and compares them with the model, giving the table in the stimulus. All the figures are constructed for this task. State what use of the normal model should be rejected or limited, give the specific evidence, and explain what further check is needed for a calibrated overall fit decision.
items.stimulus:
Region | Results recorded | Normal model predicts
--- | --- | ---
Below −0.3 mmol/L (mean − 2 sd) | 0 | about 11
−0.3 up to 0.6 mmol/L | 9 | about 68
0.6 up to 2.4 mmol/L (within 1 sd) | 431 | about 341
2.4 up to 3.3 mmol/L | 39 | about 68
3.3 mmol/L and above (mean + 2 sd) | 21 | about 11

The recorded results total 500.

answer.correct: Do not use this normal model for tail probabilities. It assigns material probability to impossible negative concentrations, while the observed counts are much thinner on the left and heavier on the far right than its symmetric predictions. Use the observations in a normal probability plot or another calibrated procedure before making a binary overall fit decision.
answer.summary: Limit or reject its tail use: impossible negative support and large directional count discrepancies expose a poor tail representation, while a calibrated overall verdict needs the observations and a suitable fit procedure.
answer.reasoning: Two standard deviations below the mean is 1.5 − 1.8 = −0.3 mmol/L. A concentration cannot be negative, so at least the roughly 11 results the model predicts below −0.3 are assigned to impossible outcomes; the model also assigns additional probability between −0.3 and zero. That structural conflict is enough to reject its use for lower-tail probabilities. The regional counts add a strong directional warning. Below 0.6 mmol/L the model expects about 11 + 68 = 79 results and the service recorded 0 + 9 = 9. Inside one standard deviation it expects about 341 and records 431. Above 3.3 mmol/L it expects about 11 and records 21. The aggregate inside two standard deviations is 479 against about 477, so combining sides conceals the mismatch. These counts support investigating right skew because the observed left tail is thin and the observed far right tail is heavy; the lower bound alone would not establish skew. Band counts are not a universal calibrated pass/fail rule, so a normal probability plot or another suitable procedure using the observations is still needed for a binary overall fit judgment.
acceptableResponses: Do not use it for tail probabilities: it predicts impossible negative concentrations, its left tail is much thinner than predicted, and it under-predicts the far right. Use a normal probability plot or calibrated procedure for an overall fit verdict.

Limit or reject the tail model. The aggregate inside two standard deviations looks close only because opposite tail errors cancel; the directional counts warn of right skew, but band counts alone are not a calibrated fit test.
commonErrors: Retaining the model because the total inside two standard deviations, 479 against about 477, is close, which is exactly the cancellation the lesson warns about.
Rejecting the model for the right reason but describing the shape as left-skewed by reading the direction of the long tail backwards.
Treating a numerical band-count difference as a universal pass/fail cutoff instead of distinguishing the support conflict, the directional warning and the need for a calibrated fit procedure.

items.prompt: Select every situation in which a binomial model for the count is defensible, given one clearly defined yes-or-no outcome per trial.

options.text: The number of 40 unrelated outpatients, each measured once, whose fasting glucose is at or above a fixed threshold, with one stated probability applying to all of them.
The number of nights above a threshold across a study in which each of 60 people contributed between 5 and 14 nights, counting every night as a trial.
The number of people in 25 households who catch a respiratory infection during one outbreak, counting each person as a trial.
The number of heads in 30 tosses of one coin whose bias is unknown but fixed for all 30 tosses.

answer.summary: The 40 outpatients and the 30 coin tosses.
answer.reasoning: The outpatient count has a fixed number of trials, a binary outcome, one probability applying to every trial, and one measurement per person, so the trials do not share a person. The coin satisfies every condition too: the probability being unknown is not a problem, because the binomial requires only that it be the same on every trial, and an unknown p can be estimated afterwards. The repeated nights fail independence, since nights from one person are clustered and knowing one night tells you a great deal about the next for that individual; treating them as separate trials manufactures precision. The household contacts fail independence for a different reason: infection spreads within a household, so one person's outcome changes their housemates' probabilities.
acceptableResponses: The 40 outpatients and the 30 coin tosses.
commonErrors: Rejecting the coin because p is unknown, when the condition is that p is constant rather than known.
Accepting the repeated nights because the total number of trials is larger and the answer looks more precise.
Accepting the household contacts because each person plainly has two possible outcomes, which is only one of the four conditions.

items.prompt: A clinic will measure 50 patients, and a model gives each one a probability of 0.20 of being at or above a chosen glucose threshold. Assuming the binomial conditions hold, give the standard deviation of the count of patients over the threshold, to two decimal places.

answer.reasoning: The standard deviation of a binomial count is the square root of np(1 − p), so √(50 × 0.20 × 0.80) = √8 = 2.83 patients. The expected count itself is np = 50 × 0.20 = 10, so a clinic planning on this model should expect about 10 patients over the threshold and should treat a result three or four either side of that as ordinary variation.
commonErrors: Answering 10, which is the mean np rather than the standard deviation.
Answering 8, which is the variance np(1 − p) with the square root omitted.
Answering 3.16 by taking the square root of np and forgetting the (1 − p) factor.

items.prompt: A diabetes service fitted a normal model to 60 patients already under its care, mean fasting glucose 142 mg/dL and standard deviation 18 mg/dL, and used it to plan clinic capacity. It now proposes to reuse the same mean, standard deviation and threshold probability to plan a community screening event open to the general public. Write a short note to the service explaining what has to change and why, using this lesson's tools. Treat the numbers as an illustrative teaching example.

answer.correct: Refit the parameters to the screening population, assess shape with that population's observations using an appropriate fit procedure, and use a binomial count only if one threshold probability is justified for independent trials; otherwise model justified strata separately.
answer.summary: The old parameters and normal shape do not transfer, and the count model also needs independent trials with a common probability before capacity can be planned.
answer.reasoning: A complete answer separates three failures. First, the parameters were fitted to people already diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and are centred at 142 mg/dL, whereas a public screening population centres much lower, so z-scores and threshold probabilities based on the old parameters would be misplaced. Second, fasting plasma glucose in a general population is empirically right-skewed, and a normal curve has no parameter that can lean; the screening observations therefore need a normal probability plot or another suitable fit procedure rather than an aggregate band-count pass. Third, a binomial capacity count requires independent trials with the same threshold probability for every person. The cohort already contains subgroups with different stipulated probabilities, so the old common value of about 0.81 cannot simply be carried over. The service should estimate probabilities for the population it will serve, justify homogeneity or model justified strata separately, and preserve one independent trial per person. The whole exercise remains illustrative rather than a recommendation about a real service.
acceptableResponses: Refit the screening population, assess its shape with an appropriate fit procedure, and use a binomial only if the people are independent and share one justified threshold probability; otherwise stratify.

The diagnosed-cohort parameters do not transfer, the general-population distribution leans right, and a common p cannot be assumed. Refit, check shape, then justify homogeneous independent trials or model strata separately.
commonErrors: Recommending only that the mean and standard deviation be recomputed, which leaves the shape failure in place.
Recommending a larger screening sample, which sharpens the estimates of parameters for a model that is the wrong shape.
Judging the refitted model acceptable on the total inside two standard deviations, when those counts are an informal diagnostic and the two tails can be wrong in opposite directions and cancel.
Using a binomial interval without checking that the same threshold probability applies to every independent trial.
Treating the illustrative capacity figures as a recommendation for a real service.

criteria.description: Selects the right expression for the quantity asked for, distinguishing a band boundary from a z-score, and a binomial mean from a binomial standard deviation.
Produces the correct value with the stated rounding, and attaches a unit where the quantity has one or omits it where the quantity is unit-free.

rubrics.title: Distinguishing what a distribution model does and does not say

criteria.description: Keeps density, area and count apart, and treats a probability for a continuous measurement as attached to a range rather than to a point.
Tests each stated condition of a model against the situation described instead of accepting the model because one condition is met.

rubrics.title: Judging whether a model may be used

criteria.description: Names the specific numerical evidence relevant to the judgment, compares tails separately rather than only in aggregate, and distinguishes a structural contradiction or strong warning from a calibrated pass/fail procedure.
Identifies the kind of failure correctly, distinguishing wrong parameters from a wrong distributional shape, and states which repairs would and would not address it.
States the limits of the conclusion, including the region of the distribution the evidence covers and the illustrative status of the example.
